clinicalPearls: Accumulation of mast cells confined to the skin, most commonly presenting in childhood
Major forms are maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis (urticaria pigmentosa), diffuse cutaneous mastocytosis and solitary mastocytoma
Stroking a lesion causes urtication and erythema (a positive Darier sign), a useful bedside clue
Childhood-onset disease often regresses around puberty, whereas adult-onset skin disease more often reflects underlying systemic mastocytosis
Mediator symptoms such as flushing and pruritus can occur, and extensive disease risks more serious reactions
Management is largely supportive with trigger avoidance and mediator-targeted therapy, reserving systemic workup for suggestive features
reference.pathophysiology: Cutaneous mastocytosis results from clonal accumulation of mast cells within the dermis, frequently associated with activating KIT mutations. The excess dermal mast cells release mediators such as histamine when mechanically or chemically triggered, producing the characteristic weal-and-flare on stroking (Darier sign) and symptoms of flushing and itch. In children the process is usually limited to the skin and tends to involute, whereas in adults cutaneous involvement is commonly a marker of systemic disease.
additionalDifferentials: Bullous disorders (in diffuse cutaneous disease of infancy)
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis with elicitation of Darier sign
Skin biopsy demonstrating increased dermal mast cells where confirmation is needed
Serum baseline tryptase to screen for systemic involvement
Assessment for systemic symptoms, especially in adults
Referral for systemic workup if features suggest systemic mastocytosis
redFlags: Adult onset raising concern for systemic mastocytosis
Systemic symptoms such as recurrent anaphylaxis or organ involvement
reference.prognosis: Childhood cutaneous mastocytosis often improves or resolves by adolescence with an excellent prognosis, whereas adult disease frequently persists and may indicate systemic mastocytosis.
pitfalls: Assuming adult cutaneous disease is skin-limited without checking for systemic mastocytosis
Provoking severe mediator release by triggering extensive lesions
Missing the Darier sign as a diagnostic clue
Overlooking anaphylaxis risk in extensive disease
management: Supportive management centred on avoiding mediator-release triggers such as heat, friction, alcohol and certain drugs including NSAIDs and opioids
H1 antihistamines for pruritus and flushing, with H2 antihistamines, the mast-cell stabiliser sodium cromoglicate or leukotriene antagonists as needed
Topical corticosteroids for symptomatic lesions and phototherapy for extensive skin disease
An adrenaline auto-injector and an anaphylaxis action plan for extensive disease at risk of severe mediator reactions
Baseline serum tryptase and assessment for systemic involvement, particularly in adult-onset disease
Reassurance that childhood disease often regresses around puberty, with referral for a systemic workup when features suggest systemic mastocytosis
